title: Trapped-ion-based quantum repeater node across a 17 km metropolitan fiber
authors: K. Fabitha, T. Runggaldier, A. Winkler, F. Bernecker, J. Bate, M. Canteri, J. Helgert, T. E. Northup, V. Krutyanskiy, B. P. Lanyon
abstract: Concatenation of quantum repeater nodes has been proposed as a means to distribute entanglement efficiently across future long-distance networks. Here, we demonstrate a trapped-ion repeater node that establishes photonic entanglement over a 17 km fiber traversing a city, moving beyond laboratory-only prototypes. The node comprises two atomic ions coupled to an optical cavity. First, a detailed characterization is performed of the long fiber channel and of ion-photon entanglement distributed across it. Next, a repeater-node protocol is implemented, achieving entanglement between a local photon and a remote photon with a Bell-state fidelity of $81.6^{+1.9}_{-1.4}\%$. These results demonstrate that trapped-ion repeater-node technology can operate over existing city-scale fiber infrastructure and represent a step toward distributed quantum repeater networks.
summary: This paper reports the successful demonstration of a trapped-ion quantum repeater node operating across a 17 km metropolitan fiber, moving quantum networking beyond controlled lab settings. The system uses trapped ions to generate and swap entanglement between local and remote photons, achieving a high Bell-state fidelity. This work validates the feasibility of using trapped-ion technology for building city-scale quantum internet infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is the efficient distribution of entanglement over long distances required for future quantum communication networks.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a trapped-ion repeater node operating over a 17 km metropolitan fiber, achieving a Bell-state fidelity of 81.6% between local and remote photons.
method: The protocol involves establishing entanglement using a trapped-ion node that couples local atomic qubits to photons distributed across the fiber, followed by Bell-state measurements.
model_or_system: The system utilizes trapped ${}^{40}	ext{Ca}^+$ ions coupled to an optical cavity, which acts as the repeater node. The setup integrates on-demand photon generation, atomic memory storage, and quantum frequency conversion (QFC) to match telecom wavelengths.
key_observables: Bell-state fidelity (81.6% $\pm$ error bars), process fidelity of polarization dynamics, and entanglement distribution rates.
important_parameters: 17 km metropolitan fiber length, 854 nm to 1550 nm wavelength conversion, and coherence times derived from fiber stability measurements.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on characterizing and mitigating environmental noise sources, including polarization drift and magnetic field fluctuations, to maintain high fidelity.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the quantum repeater node concept, the overall network setup context (including satellite imagery), and polarization dynamics measurements showing process fidelity over time.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by characterizing the deployed fiber channel, investigating ion-photon entanglement, detailing the repeater-node protocol implementation, and concluding with the results demonstrating city-scale operation.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial experimental blueprint for scaling quantum networking from lab benches to real-world infrastructure by tackling fiber-specific challenges like polarization drift and long-haul transmission.

QRN-emitted photons are detected at the two detection stations (DS), each of which contain a beam splitter (BS) and photon detectors. Dashed lines show extensions to concatenate QRNs to build repeater chains: photon detection heralds entanglement be- tween atoms in remote QRNs.
